source: NCERT Class X, Contemporary India II, Geography Ch. 2.

sections.heading: 1. Biodiversity and the Threat to It
points: India is one of the world's richest countries in **biodiversity** (flora and fauna).
Causes of decline: **habitat destruction, hunting/poaching, over-exploitation, pollution, forest fires, and invasive species**.
The greatest damage came from colonial forestry, expansion of agriculture (railways, cultivation), large development projects and mining.

sections.heading: 2. Classification of Species (IUCN)
points: **Normal species** — populations at levels for survival (e.g. cattle, sal, pine, rodents).
**Endangered species** — in danger of extinction (e.g. black buck, crocodile, Indian wild ass, sangai).
**Vulnerable species** — likely to become endangered (e.g. blue sheep, Asiatic elephant, Gangetic dolphin).
**Rare species** — small populations, may become endangered/vulnerable (e.g. Himalayan brown bear, wild Asiatic buffalo).
**Endemic species** — found only in particular areas (e.g. Andaman teal, Nicobar pigeon).
**Extinct species** — no longer found (e.g. Asiatic cheetah, pink-headed duck).

sections.heading: 3. Conservation of Forests and Wildlife
points: **Wildlife Protection Act (1972)** — legal protection to habitats and a list of protected species; banned hunting of endangered species.
**Project Tiger (1973)** — one of the best-known conservation projects; major tiger reserves include Corbett, Sunderbans, Bandhavgarh, Sariska, Periyar, Manas.
Conservation preserves ecological diversity, water, soil and genetic diversity of plants and animals.
**Reserved, Protected and Unclassed forests** — categories of forest management by the Forest Department.

sections.heading: 4. Community and Government Conservation
points: **Community participation** is central: the **Bishnoi** community of Rajasthan protects blackbuck, nilgai and trees; the **Chipko movement** resisted deforestation.
**Joint Forest Management (JFM, from 1988)** involves local communities in restoring degraded forests in return for benefits.
Sacred groves (forests of God/goddesses) protected by tribes; e.g. **Mundas and Santhals** worship trees.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Wildlife Protection Act = 1972; Project Tiger = 1973.
IUCN classes: normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic, extinct.
Asiatic cheetah, pink-headed duck = extinct in India; Sangai (Manipur brow-antlered deer) = endangered.
Bishnoi community protects blackbuck; Chipko movement = forest protection.
Joint Forest Management started 1988.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Project Tiger** was launched in **1973** (Wildlife Protection Act = **1972**).
The **Bishnoi** community is famous for protecting **blackbuck** and trees.
**Endemic** = found only in a specific area; **endangered** = in danger of extinction (do not confuse).
The **Chipko movement** was about protecting **forests/trees**.
